passages.text: CERAUNIA, or THUNDERSTONE, a name given to several kinds of stones, which the vulgar believe to fall from the clouds in thunder-storms, and to be the bolts of the thunder itself.

Of these the most common is the belemnites, or finger-stone, a long stone of a conical figure, like the point of a dart or the end of a finger, of a brown colour, and composed of fibres radiating from its axis.
Naturalists dispute much about its origin; some hold it to be a mere mineral concretion, and others the shell or the spine of some sea animal now unknown.

Others of the same name are stones in the shape of an axe or wedge, finely polished, and often bored with a hole, which are dug up in many parts of Europe. These some think the weapons or tools of ancient nations, before the use of metals was known.
The common people keep them in their houses as a preservative against lightning, and believe that a house where one is kept will never be struck.

Stones are also said by some writers to have fallen from the air in other places; but the learned generally treat these accounts as fables, or explain them by stones struck by lightning upon the ground.

A thunderstone is a prehistoric hand axe, stone tool, or fossil that was used as an amulet to protect a person or a building. The name comes from the belief that such stones fell from the sky with lightning.

Many thunderstones are polished stone axes from the Neolithic period. Scholars such as Michele Mercati in the 16th century argued that they were tools made by early people, a view that became widely accepted later.
Fossil belemnites, the bullet-shaped remains of an extinct group of squid-like animals, were also called thunderbolts or thunderstones.
Fossil sea urchins were also known as thunderstones, and in parts of England people placed them on window sills or in houses for protection.
People kept thunderstones in their homes or carried them, believing they protected against lightning and other harm.
Lightning does not create such stones. They are tools made by people or natural fossils, found in the ground.

reasons: The old headword names the thunderstone, and Wikipedia uses the same name for the folklore object.
Rare terms appear in both: belemnites, polished axes, protection from lightning.
Belemnitida scores well but covers only one kind of thunderstone.

alignments.label: Several kinds of stones

britannica.quote: a name given to several kinds of stones

wikipedia.quote: a prehistoric hand axe, stone tool, or fossil

alignments.note: Same fact in new words. Both texts apply the name to more than one kind of object.

alignments.label: Fall with lightning

britannica.quote: to fall from the clouds in thunder-storms

wikipedia.quote: Lightning does not create such stones

alignments.note: The 1778 entry gives this as a belief of the vulgar. The stones come from the ground, not from storms.

alignments.label: Dart-shaped belemnite

britannica.quote: a long stone of a conical figure, like the point of a dart

alignments.note: The description holds. Wikipedia says bullet-shaped where the 1778 entry says dart.

alignments.label: Shell of a sea animal

britannica.quote: the shell or the spine of some sea animal now unknown

wikipedia.quote: an extinct group of squid-like animals

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. The guess of a sea animal now unknown was right. The belemnite is the hard inner part of an extinct squid-like animal, not a spine.

alignments.label: Polished axes

britannica.quote: stones in the shape of an axe or wedge, finely polished

wikipedia.quote: Many thunderstones are polished stone axes from the Neolithic period

alignments.note: Same objects. Wikipedia dates them to the Neolithic.

alignments.label: Tools of ancient nations

britannica.quote: the weapons or tools of ancient nations, before the use of metals was known

wikipedia.quote: they were tools made by early people

alignments.note: The view held by some in 1778, after Mercati, is the accepted one now.

alignments.label: Guard against lightning

britannica.quote: keep them in their houses as a preservative against lightning

alignments.note: Both texts report the same custom. It is folklore: a stone in the house gives no protection.

alignments.label: Falling stones are fables

britannica.quote: the learned generally treat these accounts as fables

alignments.note: Wikipedia's thunderstone article does not cover this. Inference from other sources: stones do fall from the sky as meteorites, which scientists accepted after the fall at L'Aigle in 1803.

alignments.label: Fossil sea urchins

wikipedia.quote: Fossil sea urchins were also known as thunderstones

alignments.note: New detail. The 1778 entry does not list fossil sea urchins among the thunderstones.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1778 entry think thunderstones were?
Did thunderstones protect houses from lightning?

What did the 1778 entry think thundersto.answer: It names several kinds: the belemnite or finger-stone [B2], and polished stone axes that some took for tools of ancient nations [B4]. Wikipedia agrees: thunderstones are stone tools or fossils [W1], many of them Neolithic axes [W2].

What is a belemnite?.answer: The 1778 entry describes a dart-shaped stone and reports a dispute about its origin, with some calling it the shell of an unknown sea animal [B2] [B3]. Wikipedia says it is the remains of an extinct group of squid-like animals [W3].

Did thunderstones protect houses from li.answer: No. The 1778 entry reports that common people kept them for that purpose [B5]. Wikipedia describes the same custom as folklore [W5], and says lightning does not create such stones [W6].
